Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_default_group.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn take(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(take)) } /// Every bare-name subscription of this broker reads in the group `workers`. #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").default_group("workers")) } examples/manual/redis_broker_default_group.rs struct Take; impl Handle<Order> for Take { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(subscriber("orders", Take).build())) } /// Every bare-name subscription of this broker reads in the group `workers`. fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").default_group("workers")) }

RedisError is the one error type of the crate: connect, publish, subscribe, stream reads, shutdown, transactions and refused options. Each variant names the step that failed. The fred error behind it is its source, so the client library's types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Connect the address could not be parsed, the server did not answer, or the login was refused Publish the server refused a write, such as a list push to a key that holds a stream (WRONGTYPE) Subscribe a consumer group could not be created, or a subscription could not open Stream a stream read or an acknowledgement failed ShutDown a publisher, a delivery or a transaction was used after the broker shut down InvalidOptions the settings cannot work together, such as a bare name with no default group ServerTooOld a claiming subscription met a server older than Redis 8.4 TransactionBusy, NoTransaction a transaction was begun twice on one publisher, or ended with none open Flush a pipelined window failed to send what it owed A service meets the error in two places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads anything. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

A ledger entry the server refuses is logged with its cause, and the order is settled as a retry. The subscription claims the order back once it has been idle thirty seconds. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_errors.rs /// A retried order stays pending and comes back once it has been idle for thirty seconds. #[subscriber(RedisStream::claiming("orders", Duration::from_secs(30)).group("workers"))] async fn book(order: &Order, Out(ledger): Out<impl Publisher, Ledger>) -> HandlerOutcome { let entry = LedgerEntry { order_id: order.id, amount: order.amount, }; if let Err(err) = ledger.message(&entry).publish().await { // The error carries the server's answer, such as `WRONGTYPE`. tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "ledger entry not written"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/redis_broker_errors.rs struct Book; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Book where Entry: OutEntry<Ledger, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let entry = LedgerEntry { order_id: order.id, amount: order.amount, }; if let Err(err) = outs.get(Ledger).message(&entry).publish().await { // The error carries the server's answer, such as `WRONGTYPE`. tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "ledger entry not written"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } /// A retried order stays pending and comes back once it has been idle for thirty seconds. fn orders() -> RedisStream { RedisStream::claiming("orders", Duration::from_secs(30)).group("workers") }

RedisBroker::from_pool wraps a fred Pool the service built itself, for client settings the broker's own builders do not reach. fred's Builder sets what the broker leaves at fred's defaults: a command timeout, a reconnection policy, buffer sizes, any topology a fred Config describes. The service builds the pool in its #[ruststream::app] builder and hands it over unconnected. The broker dials it when the service starts, and an unreachable server fails the start, as it does for a broker built from an address. A pool the service has already connected is adopted as it is. The pool's size is the pool of the broker. Each subscription's own connection is built from the pool's config and reconnects by the pool's policy. The generated document reports no host for such a broker, because the address sits inside the pool's own config. A TestApp test runs the same app in process: it reads the pool's size and config and dials nothing.

The dependency line: fred = "10" The pool holds eight connections, bounds every command at two seconds and reconnects every half second. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_from_pool.rs /// Eight connections, a two-second bound on every command, and a reconnect every half second. fn pool(url: &str) -> Result<Pool, FredError> { Builder::from_config(Config::from_url(url)?) .with_performance_config(|performance| { performance.default_command_timeout = Duration::from_secs(2); }) .set_policy(ReconnectPolicy::new_constant(0, 500)) .build_pool(8) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { // A constant URL and a non-zero size: the pool always builds. let pool = pool("redis://localhost:6379").expect("a pool over a valid URL"); // The pool is not connected here: the broker dials it when the service starts. service(RedisBroker::from_pool(pool)) } examples/manual/redis_broker_from_pool.rs /// Eight connections, a two-second bound on every command, and a reconnect every half second. fn pool(url: &str) -> Result<Pool, FredError> { Builder::from_config(Config::from_url(url)?) .with_performance_config(|performance| { performance.default_command_timeout = Duration::from_secs(2); }) .set_policy(ReconnectPolicy::new_constant(0, 500)) .build_pool(8) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { // A constant URL and a non-zero size: the pool always builds. let pool = pool("redis://localhost:6379").expect("a pool over a valid URL"); // The pool is not connected here: the broker dials it when the service starts. service(RedisBroker::from_pool(pool)) }

pool sets how many connections publishes, settlements and handler commands share; each subscription reads on a connection of its own. The pool holds 4 connections unless the service sets another number. Replies, acknowledgements, retries and the commands a handler sends through FredPool take turns on them. Each stream and list subscription reads on one more connection, and each Pub/Sub subscription listens on one. So a blocking read never holds up a publish, and a service opens the pool plus one connection per subscription. A pool of zero connections fails startup. A TestApp test keeps the pool size, and refuses zero the same way.

The service answers each order with a receipt through a pool of sixteen connections. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_pool.rs /// Sixteen pooled connections for the replies and acknowledgements of a busy service. #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").pool(16)) } examples/manual/redis_broker_pool.rs /// Sixteen pooled connections for the replies and acknowledgements of a busy service. fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").pool(16)) }

Each form has a prelude with its policy under the name Publish; ruststream_fred::prelude serves a file that mixes forms. A service on one form globs that form's prelude: stream::prelude, list::prelude or pubsub::prelude. Each carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds RedisBroker, the form's descriptors and their options, the form's context types, and the capabilities the form offers. The form's policy comes under the name every broker crate uses, Publish, so a mount site reads the same on every broker. The stream prelude also brings TransactionalPublish, the seek types and the keys module of context keys. ruststream_fred::prelude is for a file that mixes forms. It holds the same items for all three forms, with the policies under their prefixed names, RedisPublish, RedisListPublish and RedisPubSubPublish. It also brings the stream, list and pubsub modules, so a mixed file writes stream::Publish beside pubsub::Publish. It has no bare Publish, because one name would stand for three types. A handler body names only the capability it needs, such as Out<impl Publisher>, so moving a handler between forms changes the descriptor and not the handler. The one exception is a body that sets a per-message setting: it names RedisPublishOptions in its bound, from this crate's prelude.

A stream subscription replies onto a Pub/Sub channel, and a channel subscription hears the reply. The one glob brings both descriptors and the pubsub module the reply policy comes from. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_fred::prelude::*; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments")] struct Shipped { order_id: u64, } #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"), reply)] async fn ship(order: &Order) -> Shipped { Shipped { order_id: order.id } } #[subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("shipments"))] async fn notify(shipped: &Shipped) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(shipped.order_id, "customer notified"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { // Each form's policy under its module: `stream::Publish`, `list::Publish`, `pubsub::Publish`. b.include(ship) .out_reply(pubsub::Publish::new()) .include(notify) }, ) } examples/manual/redis_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_fred::prelude::*; struct Ship; impl Handle<Order, Shipped> for Ship { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Shipped, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Shipped { order_id: order.id })) } } struct Notify; impl Handle<Shipped> for Notify { fn handle( &self, shipped: &Shipped, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(shipped.order_id, "customer notified"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { // Each form's policy under its module: `stream::Publish`, `list::Publish`, `pubsub::Publish`. b.include( subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"), Ship) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(pubsub::Publish::new()) .include(subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("shipments"), Notify).build()) }, ) }

sentinel_credentials and sentinel_password log in to the sentinels with a pair of their own, apart from the data nodes. A Sentinel deployment may protect the sentinels and the primary separately. The client asks the sentinels where the primary is, logged in with sentinel_credentials, and then logs in to the primary with credentials. sentinel_password is the form with a password and no user. Both come with the sentinel-auth feature and apply to the sentinel topology only. A TestApp test runs no handshake, so it proves the service starts and works with both pairs set.

The dependency line: ruststream-fred = { version = "0.8", features = ["sentinel-auth"] } The primary checks the user worker, and the sentinels the user monitor. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_sentinel_auth.rs /// The data nodes check the user `worker`, the sentinels the user `monitor`. fn broker(data_password: &str, sentinel_password: &str) -> RedisBroker { RedisBroker::sentinel( "mymaster", ["sentinel-1.internal:26379", "sentinel-2.internal:26379"], ) .credentials("worker", data_password) .sentinel_credentials("monitor", sentinel_password) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let data_password = env::var("REDIS_PASSWORD").unwrap_or_default(); let sentinel_password = env::var("SENTINEL_PASSWORD").unwrap_or_default(); service(broker(&data_password, &sentinel_password)) } examples/manual/redis_broker_sentinel_auth.rs /// The data nodes check the user `worker`, the sentinels the user `monitor`. fn broker(data_password: &str, sentinel_password: &str) -> RedisBroker { RedisBroker::sentinel( "mymaster", ["sentinel-1.internal:26379", "sentinel-2.internal:26379"], ) .credentials("worker", data_password) .sentinel_credentials("monitor", sentinel_password) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let data_password = env::var("REDIS_PASSWORD").unwrap_or_default(); let sentinel_password = env::var("SENTINEL_PASSWORD").unwrap_or_default(); service(broker(&data_password, &sentinel_password)) }

RedisBroker::sentinel names the monitored primary and the sentinels that watch it; the client finds the primary through them. The first argument is the name the sentinels monitor the primary under, such as mymaster. The second is the sentinels, each a host:port address; a sentinel without a port means 26379. At startup the client asks the sentinels where the primary is and connects to it. Every read and every write goes to the primary. After a failover the connections reconnect, and the client asks the sentinels again, so the service follows the new primary. A sentinel list carries no password. The primary's password goes in credentials, and the sentinels' own in sentinel_credentials.

The service reaches the primary mymaster through either of two sentinels. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_sentinel.rs /// The primary `mymaster`, found through either of two sentinels. fn broker() -> RedisBroker { RedisBroker::sentinel( "mymaster", ["sentinel-1.internal:26379", "sentinel-2.internal:26379"], ) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker()) } examples/manual/redis_broker_sentinel.rs /// The primary `mymaster`, found through either of two sentinels. fn broker() -> RedisBroker { RedisBroker::sentinel( "mymaster", ["sentinel-1.internal:26379", "sentinel-2.internal:26379"], ) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker()) }

Shutdown unblocks every read and closes every connection; a publisher used afterwards gets RedisError::ShutDown at once. When the service stops, the runtime runs the on_shutdown hooks while the broker is still connected and then shuts the broker down. A stream or list subscription may be waiting in a blocking read on its own connection. The broker sends CLIENT UNBLOCK for each such read, so the read ends at once instead of at its timeout, and closes the connection. Then the pool sends QUIT on every connection, and the after_shutdown hooks run. A publisher taken before the shutdown keeps pointing at the closed connection. A publish through it, an acknowledgement of a delivery or a transaction returns RedisError::ShutDown, and never runs against the dead pool. A tool that drives the broker by hand receives a ClosedRedisBroker from the shutdown; its connections_closed is the number of pooled connections it closed.

The service answers each order with a shipment, and logs once its connections are closed. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_shutdown.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(ship) }) // Runs once every connection of the broker is closed. .after_shutdown(async move |_state| { tracing::info!("redis connections closed"); Ok::<_, Infallible>(()) }) } examples/manual/redis_broker_shutdown.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include( subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"), Ship) .reply() .build(), ) }) // Runs once every connection of the broker is closed. .after_shutdown(async move |_state| { tracing::info!("redis connections closed"); Ok::<_, Infallible>(()) }) }

tls takes a TlsConnector or a TlsConfig on any topology; a rediss:// or valkeys:// URL switches TLS on for a standalone server. TLS comes with one of three features, all off by default. tls-rustls builds on rustls with the aws-lc-rs crypto provider, tls-rustls-ring on rustls with ring, and tls-native-tls on the platform's own TLS library. The features add to each other rather than exclude each other. The crate re-exports TlsConnector and TlsConfig from fred, so a service names them without a dependency on fred. TlsConnector::default_rustls() trusts the system's root certificates and presents no client certificate. It reads the certificates from the system and can fail, so the connector is built in main before the service starts. A connector built from a rustls ClientConfig carries a private certificate authority or a client certificate. Every connection of the broker uses it, the subscriptions' own included. A TestApp test runs no handshake, so it proves the service starts and works with the connector in place.

The dependency line: ruststream-fred = { version = "0.8", features = ["tls-rustls"] } The service reaches a cluster over TLS and logs in as the ACL user worker. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_tls.rs /// The cluster over TLS, logged in as the ACL user `worker`. fn broker(tls: TlsConnector, password: &str) -> RedisBroker { RedisBroker::cluster(["redis-1.internal:6380", "redis-2.internal:6380"]) .credentials("worker", password) .tls(tls) } #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // The system's trust roots, and no client certificate. let tls = TlsConnector::default_rustls()?; let password = env::var("REDIS_PASSWORD")?; service(broker(tls, &password)).run().await?; Ok(()) } examples/manual/redis_broker_tls.rs /// The cluster over TLS, logged in as the ACL user `worker`. fn broker(tls: TlsConnector, password: &str) -> RedisBroker { RedisBroker::cluster(["redis-1.internal:6380", "redis-2.internal:6380"]) .credentials("worker", password) .tls(tls) } #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // The system's trust roots, and no client certificate. let tls = TlsConnector::default_rustls()?; let password = env::var("REDIS_PASSWORD")?; service(broker(tls, &password)).run().await?; Ok(()) }

StreamContext gives a stream handler the entry id, the position that redelivers it, the consumer group and the group's seek handle. The subscription builds it once per delivery, beside the payload and the headers. A handler names it as its context type, ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamContext>, and reads a field with ctx.context(key). A handler that needs one field binds it as a parameter with Ctx<K> instead. Each key is a type in context::keys, and the stream prelude brings the module in as keys: Key Value What it is EntryId EntryId the <milliseconds>-<sequence> id the entry was read at; it orders the way the stream does Position RedisGroupPosition the group cursor that delivers this entry again ConsumerGroup &str the group the subscription reads through, as ConsumerGroup shows SeekHandle RedisGroupSeeker the handle that moves the whole group to another position FredPool fred::clients::Pool the broker's connection pool, as FredPool shows Each key is a zero-sized type, and reading it is a plain field access the compiler resolves: no hashing, no boxing, no downcast. A key belongs to the context types that carry its field, so a key read off the wrong form's context does not compile. A batch handler reads StreamBatchContext, a Pub/Sub handler PubSubContext. A list delivery carries its payload and headers alone; a list handler reads the pool through FredPool or keeps the default () context. The two claiming read modes report a delivery's count and idle time as the DELIVERY_COUNT_HEADER and IDLE_MS_HEADER headers, which every transport reads the same way. A context costs a handler that does not name one nothing: the default () context builds no value.

The handler writes where each order sat in the stream, and which group read it, to an order trail. Macros Manual examples/redis_context_stream.rs /// Reads the entry id and the consumer group off the delivery's context. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("audit"), reply)] async fn trace(order: &Order, ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamContext>) -> Trail { let entry_id = ctx.context(keys::EntryId); let group = ctx.context(keys::ConsumerGroup); tracing::info!(order.id, %entry_id, group, "order traced"); Trail { order_id: order.id, entry_id: entry_id.to_string(), group: group.to_owned(), } } examples/manual/redis_context_stream.rs /// Reads the entry id and the consumer group off the delivery's context. struct Trace; impl Handle<Order, Trail, (), StreamContext> for Trace { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Trail, HandlerOutcome>> { let entry_id = ctx.context(keys::EntryId); let group = ctx.context(keys::ConsumerGroup); tracing::info!(order.id, %entry_id, group, "order traced"); ready(Ok(Trail { order_id: order.id, entry_id: entry_id.to_string(), group: group.to_owned(), })) } }

A stream batch handler's context, StreamBatchContext, carries only the consumer group and the seek handle, which belong to the whole subscription. A batch spans many entries, so a field that differs per entry has no single value for it. The body reads the batch's fields with ctx.context(key): keys::ConsumerGroup, keys::SeekHandle and keys::FredPool. A Ctx<K> parameter binds the per-delivery context, so a batch body reads its fields off the context instead. The handler names the context in its signature, ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamBatchContext>, beside a slice payload. The batch itself is the read's COUNT: .batch(n) at the mount site asks Redis for up to n entries per XREADGROUP.

The batch is billed in one call, and every invoice records the group, read once off the batch's context. Macros Manual examples/redis_context_batch.rs /// Bills a batch of orders; the group is read once, off the batch's context. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("billing"), reply)] async fn bill_all( orders: &[Order], ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamBatchContext>, ) -> Result<Vec<Invoice>, HandlerOutcome> { let group = ctx.context(keys::ConsumerGroup); tracing::info!(orders = orders.len(), group, "batch billed"); Ok(orders .iter() .map(|order| Invoice { order_id: order.id, billed_by: group.to_owned(), }) .collect()) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(bill_all.batch(nonzero!(32))).out_reply(Publish) }) } examples/manual/redis_context_batch.rs /// Bills a batch of orders; the group is read once, off the batch's context. struct BillAll; impl Handle<[Order], Vec<Invoice>, (), StreamBatchContext> for BillAll { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamBatchContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Vec<Invoice>, Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let group = ctx.context(keys::ConsumerGroup); tracing::info!(orders = orders.len(), group, "batch billed"); ready(Ok(orders .iter() .map(|order| Invoice { order_id: order.id, billed_by: group.to_owned(), }) .collect())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { let bill_all = subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("billing"), BillAll); b.include(bill_all.batch(nonzero!(32)).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish) }, ) }

Ctx<keys::ConsumerGroup> binds the consumer group a stream subscription reads through, on a single delivery or a batch. The group is fixed when the subscription opens: the descriptor's .group(..), or the broker's default_group for a subscription that names none. A handler that reads it learns the group at run time, so one body serves whichever group it is mounted under. As a Ctx parameter the key yields an owned String. Read off a context with ctx.context(keys::ConsumerGroup), it yields a &str borrowed from the context. A batch body reads it that way off StreamBatchContext, since the group belongs to the whole subscription.

The subscription names only the stream; the group comes from the broker's default, and each invoice records it. Macros Manual examples/redis_context_consumer_group.rs #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn bill(order: &Order, Ctx(group): Ctx<keys::ConsumerGroup>) -> Invoice { tracing::info!(order.id, %group, "order billed"); Invoice { order_id: order.id, billed_by: group, } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").default_group("billing"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(bill).out_reply(Publish)) } examples/manual/redis_context_consumer_group.rs struct Bill; impl Handle<Order, Invoice, (), StreamContext> for Bill { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Invoice, HandlerOutcome>> { let group = ctx.context(keys::ConsumerGroup); tracing::info!(order.id, group, "order billed"); ready(Ok(Invoice { order_id: order.id, billed_by: group.to_owned(), })) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").default_group("billing"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Bill).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish) }) }

Ctx<keys::FredPool> hands a handler the broker's fred connection pool on every form, for a command whose answer it needs now. The value is fred::clients::Pool, the pool the broker publishes through. A command sent on it runs at once, and the handler reads its reply before it returns. That is the difference from a pipelined command, which leaves after the handler, with the delivery's acknowledgement, and returns no reply. The command methods come from fred's interface traits, such as fred::interfaces::KeysInterface, which the handler's file imports. As the only Ctx key of a handler, FredPool names PoolContext, a context that carries the pool alone. Beside a form's own key it reads that form's context: StreamContext, StreamBatchContext, PubSubContext or the pipelined PipelineContext. There it goes after the form's key in the signature, because the first Ctx key names the handler's context. A list handler, whose delivery carries no context of its own, takes the pool through PoolContext.

Each order takes the next number of a shared sequence with INCR, and the reply carries it. Macros Manual examples/redis_context_fred_pool.rs /// Numbers each order with `INCR`, whose answer the reply carries. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("numbering"), reply)] async fn assign_number( order: &Order, Ctx(pool): Ctx<keys::FredPool>, ) -> Result<Numbered, HandlerOutcome> { match pool.incr::<i64, _>("orders:sequence").await { Ok(number) => Ok(Numbered { order_id: order.id, number, }), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "the sequence is out of reach"); Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } } examples/manual/redis_context_fred_pool.rs /// Numbers each order with `INCR`, whose answer the reply carries. struct AssignNumber; impl Handle<Order, Numbered, (), PoolContext> for AssignNumber { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PoolContext>, ) -> Result<Numbered, HandlerOutcome> { let pool = ctx.context(keys::FredPool); match pool.incr::<i64, _>("orders:sequence").await { Ok(number) => Ok(Numbered { order_id: order.id, number, }), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "the sequence is out of reach"); Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } } }

PubSubContext gives a channel handler the channel a message arrived on and whether a pattern matched it. The subscription builds it once per message, on a RedisPubSub channel and a RedisPubSubPattern glob alike. On a channel subscription the channel is the one it names. On a pattern subscription it is the concrete channel the glob matched, so it differs from message to message. Key Value What it is Channel &str the channel the message was published to FromPattern bool true when a PSUBSCRIBE glob matched the message FredPool fred::clients::Pool the broker's connection pool, as FredPool shows A handler names the context in its signature, ctx: &mut Context<'_, PubSubContext>, and reads each field with ctx.context(key). A pattern subscription names where its retry copies go with out_retry, because a glob is no channel a copy could be published to.

One handler hears every events.* channel and records the channel each event came from. Macros Manual examples/redis_context_pubsub.rs /// Hears every `events.*` channel and records which one each event came from. #[subscriber(RedisPubSubPattern::new("events.*"), reply)] async fn hear(event: &Event, ctx: &mut Context<'_, PubSubContext>) -> Heard { let channel = ctx.context(keys::Channel); tracing::info!(event.id, channel, "event heard"); Heard { event_id: event.id, channel: channel.to_owned(), from_pattern: ctx.context(keys::FromPattern), } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("events", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { // A pattern names no channel a retry could go back to, so the mount names one. b.include(hear) .out_reply(stream::Publish) .out_retry(pubsub::Publish::new()) .to("events.retry") }, ) } examples/manual/redis_context_pubsub.rs /// Hears every `events.*` channel and records which one each event came from. struct Hear; impl Handle<Event, Heard, (), PubSubContext> for Hear { fn handle( &self, event: &Event, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PubSubContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Heard, HandlerOutcome>> { let channel = ctx.context(keys::Channel); tracing::info!(event.id, channel, "event heard"); ready(Ok(Heard { event_id: event.id, channel: channel.to_owned(), from_pattern: ctx.context(keys::FromPattern), })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("events", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { let hear = subscriber(RedisPubSubPattern::new("events.*"), Hear); // A pattern names no channel a retry could go back to, so the mount names one. b.include(hear.reply().build()) .out_reply(stream::Publish) .out_retry(pubsub::Publish::new()) .to("events.retry") }, ) }

RedisList is a work queue: each entry goes to one consumer, and the simple form pops it with BRPOP and settles nothing. RedisList::new("thumbnails") reads the list thumbnails. A producer pushes an entry with LPUSH, and a consumer pops it from the other end, so entries arrive in the order they were pushed. Each entry reaches exactly one consumer: a list has no consumer groups, no fan-out and no replay. Consumers of one list in several processes share its entries. The simple form pops the entry with BRPOP, which removes it from Redis. A handler that crashes after the pop loses the entry, so delivery is at most once. The outcome settles nothing: an ack, a retry and a drop all report AckError::Unsupported, and the runtime logs a warning for each. A list that has to keep an entry until its handler finishes uses the reliable form. How long one pop waits on the server is the subscription's block setting, five seconds by default.

Thumbnails are cheap to make again, so a lost job costs nothing. Macros Manual examples/redis_lists.rs /// Each entry of `thumbnails` reaches one consumer. It left Redis when it was popped, so the /// outcome settles nothing. #[subscriber(RedisList::new("thumbnails"))] async fn make_thumbnail(job: &Job) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "thumbnail made"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/redis_lists.rs /// Each entry of `thumbnails` reaches one consumer. It left Redis when it was popped, so the /// outcome settles nothing. struct MakeThumbnail; impl Handle<Job, (), (), (), AppState> for MakeThumbnail { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.id, "thumbnail made"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn thumbnails() -> RedisList { RedisList::new("thumbnails") }

processing names the list an entry waits on while handled; on a cluster both keys share one hash tag, or the subscription refuses to start. The processing list is where a reliable subscription moves an entry before its handler runs. Its default name is the queue's key with .processing appended, so jobs waits on jobs.processing. Every consumer of the queue that uses the same name shares that list. On a cluster a claim moves the entry between the two keys in one command, and Redis refuses a command that spans hash slots. A hash tag puts both keys on one slot: Redis hashes only the part between { and }, so {exports} and {exports}.in-flight land together. The default name follows the tag of its queue. A subscription whose two keys hash to different slots does not start, and its error names the tag to use.

The export queue runs on a cluster, and its processing list carries the queue's tag. Macros Manual examples/redis_lists_processing.rs /// `{exports}` is the hash tag of both keys, so the queue and its processing list live on one /// slot of the cluster. #[subscriber( RedisList::new("{exports}") .reliable() .processing("{exports}.in-flight") )] async fn export(job: &Export) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "export written"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("exports", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::cluster(["redis://localhost:7000"]), |b| { b.include(export) }) } examples/manual/redis_lists_processing.rs /// `{exports}` is the hash tag of both keys, so the queue and its processing list live on one /// slot of the cluster. fn exports() -> RedisList { RedisList::new("{exports}") .reliable() .processing("{exports}.in-flight") } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("exports", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::cluster(["redis://localhost:7000"]), |b| { b.include(subscriber(exports(), WriteExport).build()) }) }

recovery_zset starts a watchdog that returns entries a dead consumer left on its processing list, once idle min_idle. A reliable list keeps no idle time of its own, so the subscription records every claim in the named sorted set, scored by the time of the claim. Each read of the subscription sweeps the set and pushes an entry claimed more than min_idle ago back onto the queue, where a live consumer takes it. An ack or a drop removes the entry's record from the set. min_idle has no default, and a recovery set without it does not start. It has to exceed the longest time one entry takes to handle: a slower handler has its entry returned and handled twice. The sweep runs once per read, so the block interval sets how soon a due entry returns, and one pass moves at most 128 entries. recovery_ttl expires the set once no claim refreshes it, and it has to exceed min_idle. recovery_zset turns the reliable form on by itself.

An invoice claimed by a worker that died is sent by another one a minute later. Macros Manual examples/redis_lists.rs /// Every claim is recorded in `invoices.claims`. An entry still unsettled after `MIN_IDLE` goes /// back on `invoices`, so set it above the longest time one invoice takes. #[subscriber( RedisList::new("invoices") .reliable() .min_idle(MIN_IDLE) .recovery_zset("invoices.claims") )] async fn send_invoice(job: &Job) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "invoice sent"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/redis_lists.rs /// Every claim is recorded in `invoices.claims`. An entry still unsettled after `MIN_IDLE` goes /// back on `invoices`, so set it above the longest time one invoice takes. struct SendInvoice; impl Handle<Job, (), (), (), AppState> for SendInvoice { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.id, "invoice sent"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn invoices() -> RedisList { RedisList::new("invoices") .reliable() .min_idle(MIN_IDLE) .recovery_zset("invoices.claims") }

reliable moves each entry to a processing list and removes it on ack, which makes the queue at-least-once. The subscription claims an entry with BLMOVE, which moves it from the queue to the processing list in one command. The entry stays there while the handler runs. An ack removes it with LREM. A retry pushes it back onto the queue with LPUSH, behind the entries already waiting, and then removes it from the processing list. A crash between those two commands leaves the entry in both lists, so it is handled twice rather than lost. A drop removes it, as an ack does. A consumer that dies after the move leaves its entry on the processing list; a recovery set returns such entries to the queue.

The render farm turns the first job away while it warms up, so that job goes back on the queue and is rendered when it is popped again. Macros Manual examples/redis_lists.rs /// The entry waits on a processing list while the handler runs: an ack removes it, a retry puts /// it back onto `renders`, behind the jobs waiting there. #[subscriber(RedisList::new("renders").reliable())] async fn render(job: &Job, State(farm): State<RenderFarm>) -> HandlerOutcome { match farm.render(job).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(job.id, %err, "render failed, back on the queue"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/redis_lists.rs /// The entry waits on a processing list while the handler runs: an ack removes it, a retry puts /// it back onto `renders`, behind the jobs waiting there. struct Render; impl Handle<Job, (), (), (), AppState> for Render { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if let Err(err) = ctx.state().farm.render(job).await { tracing::warn!(job.id, %err, "render failed, back on the queue"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } fn renders() -> RedisList { RedisList::new("renders").reliable() }

.pipeline() settles a subscription in a window, and a handler queues its own Redis commands to leave with its acknowledgement. The step chains where the handler is mounted, b.include(handler.pipeline()), like .workers(..) or .block(..). It applies to a RedisStream, a RedisList, a RedisPubSub and a RedisPubSubPattern, and keeps every setting the descriptor carries. Each form's prelude brings the step in with RedisPipelineSteps, together with the InRound transform and the Bindable bound. A handler takes the delivery's round with Ctx<keys::Pipeline>, a RedisPipeline. What it queues there runs after the handler returns, in one pipeline with the settles of the whole window: under load, one round trip per fetched batch instead of one per command. The queued commands follow the delivery's outcome: they leave when the delivery is acknowledged and are dropped otherwise. So a handler's Redis side effects never land for a delivery that comes back. The Window page draws a window from the read to the flush. A handler that reads Ctx<keys::Pipeline> and is mounted without .pipeline() does not compile. The error is the framework's general one: the handler's context, PipelineContext, does not match the subscription's. A delivery whose handler queues nothing costs the window no buffer. .atomic() after the step makes each delivery's segment a transaction.

An accepted order is recorded on a list in the same round trip as its XACK; an order without items is dropped, and its push with it. Macros Manual examples/redis_pipelining.rs /// Records an accepted order on the `orders:accepted` list, in the same round trip as its `XACK`. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"))] async fn accept(order: &Order, Ctx(pipeline): Ctx<keys::Pipeline>) -> HandlerOutcome { if pipeline .lpush("orders:accepted", order.id.to_string()) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } if order.items == 0 { // The delivery is dropped, and the push queued above goes with it. tracing::warn!(order.id, "an order without items is dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(accept.pipeline()) }) } examples/manual/redis_pipelining.rs /// Records an accepted order on the `orders:accepted` list, in the same round trip as its `XACK`. struct Accept; impl Handle<Order, (), (), PipelineContext> for Accept { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PipelineContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let pipeline = ctx.context(keys::Pipeline); if pipeline .lpush("orders:accepted", order.id.to_string()) .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } if order.items == 0 { // The delivery is dropped, and the push queued above goes with it. tracing::warn!(order.id, "an order without items is dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(()) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { let accept = subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"), Accept); b.include(accept.pipeline().build()) }, ) }

.atomic() after .pipeline() wraps each delivery's commands and settle in MULTI and EXEC, so they apply together or not at all. The step follows .pipeline() at the mount site: b.include(handler.pipeline().atomic()). A delivery's segment becomes MULTI, the commands its handler queued, the delivery's settle where the form has one, and EXEC. The transaction still travels inside the window's pipeline, so it costs no round trip of its own. A handler's side effects and its acknowledgement are then one unit: a reader never sees the effects of an entry that is still pending. .atomic() without .pipeline() does not compile, and the error says to write .pipeline().atomic(). The transaction is Redis's, with Redis's limits. A command that fails inside EXEC, a WRONGTYPE for example, leaves the other commands of the block executed: Redis does not roll back. On a cluster, a transaction runs only when every key in it hashes to one slot, the slot of the subscription's key. A hash tag gives the handler's keys that slot: {orders}:invoices beside a stream {orders}. A command for another slot makes Redis refuse the whole EXEC, so a segment never runs in part.

An invoice is queued beside each paid order and leaves in one MULTI / EXEC with the order's XACK. Macros Manual examples/redis_pipelining_atomic.rs /// Queues an invoice beside the order; the hash tag `{orders}` keeps both keys on one cluster slot. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("{orders}").group("billing"))] async fn invoice(order: &Order, Ctx(pipeline): Ctx<keys::Pipeline>) -> HandlerOutcome { if pipeline .lpush("{orders}:invoices", order.id.to_string()) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } if !order.paid { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an unpaid order gets no invoice"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(invoice.pipeline().atomic()) }) } examples/manual/redis_pipelining_atomic.rs /// Queues an invoice beside the order; the hash tag `{orders}` keeps both keys on one cluster slot. struct Invoice; impl Handle<Order, (), (), PipelineContext> for Invoice { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PipelineContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let pipeline = ctx.context(keys::Pipeline); if pipeline .lpush("{orders}:invoices", order.id.to_string()) .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } if !order.paid { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an unpaid order gets no invoice"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(()) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { let invoice = subscriber(RedisStream::new("{orders}").group("billing"), Invoice); b.include(invoice.pipeline().atomic().build()) }, ) }

pipeline.bind(out) makes a slot's publishes join the delivery's round, so they leave only if the delivery is acknowledged. The handler takes the slot as Out<impl Bindable>, where Bindable is the bound every publisher of this crate meets. bind hands the slot back with its codec and transforms, and every publish through it from then on is queued into the round. A bound publish leaves with the delivery's settle, after the commands the handler queued before it. A slot publish the handler does not bind leaves at once, whatever the delivery's outcome. The slot's policy is one of this crate's: stream::Publish, list::Publish or pubsub::Publish; another broker's publisher does not compile there. A reply joins the round through the InRound transform.

The handler writes an order's first step to the order log through a bound slot, so a dropped order leaves no entry. Macros Manual examples/redis_pipelining_round.rs #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"), reply)] async fn accept( order: &Order, Ctx(pipeline): Ctx<keys::Pipeline>, Out(out): Out<impl Bindable>, ) -> Result<LogEntry, HandlerOutcome> { // Bound to the round, the entry leaves with the acknowledgement, and not without it. let log = pipeline.bind(out); let accepted = LogEntry { id: order.id, step: Step::Accepted, }; if log.message(&accepted).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } if order.items == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an order without items is dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(LogEntry { id: order.id, step: Step::Confirmed, }) } examples/manual/redis_pipelining_round.rs struct Accept; impl<Log> Handle<Order, LogEntry, Outs<(Log,)>, PipelineContext> for Accept where Log: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Bindable>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Log,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, PipelineContext>, ) -> Result<LogEntry, HandlerOutcome> { // Bound to the round, the entry leaves with the acknowledgement, and not without it. let log = ctx.context(keys::Pipeline).bind(outs.get(DefaultSlot)); let accepted = LogEntry { id: order.id, step: Step::Accepted, }; if log.message(&accepted).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } if order.items == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an order without items is dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(LogEntry { id: order.id, step: Step::Confirmed, }) } }

RedisPipeline queues fred's commands, Lua through eval and evalsha, and any other command through custom; a reply is not read back. The pipeline carries fred's command methods for keys, strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, functions and PUBLISH, under fred's names and arguments. Each method queues its command into the delivery's segment and returns Result<(), fred::error::Error>. Ok means queued; an error is fred's refusal at queue time, such as an argument that does not convert. The command runs after the handler returns, so its reply never reaches the handler. A command whose answer the handler needs runs on the pool instead, through FredPool. eval queues a Lua script by its source and evalsha by its SHA1 digest, each with its keys and arguments. On a cluster a script goes to the node of its first key. custom queues any command by name, for one the methods do not cover. The first command a delivery queues opens a fred pipeline for it; a delivery that queues nothing allocates none. The in-process Redis of the test harness runs no scripts, so a test of a script runs against a server.

The handler queues two commands: a push onto the shipping queue and a counter. Macros Manual examples/redis_pipelining_commands.rs /// Puts the order on the shipping queue and counts it, both in the delivery's round. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"))] async fn ship(order: &Order, Ctx(pipeline): Ctx<keys::Pipeline>) -> HandlerOutcome { // `Ok` means queued: the commands run after this handler acknowledges the delivery. if pipeline .lpush("shipments", order.id.to_string()) .await .is_err() || pipeline .hincrby("orders:totals", "shipped", 1) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/redis_pipelining_commands.rs /// Puts the order on the shipping queue and counts it, both in the delivery's round. struct Ship; impl Handle<Order, (), (), PipelineContext> for Ship { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PipelineContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let pipeline = ctx.context(keys::Pipeline); // `Ok` means queued: the commands run after this handler acknowledges the delivery. if pipeline .lpush("shipments", order.id.to_string()) .await .is_err() || pipeline .hincrby("orders:totals", "shipped", 1) .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } The same two writes as one Lua script, so that no client sees one without the other: Macros Manual examples/redis_pipelining_commands.rs /// The same two writes as one Lua script, so no client sees one without the other. const SHIP_AND_COUNT: &str = "redis.call('HINCRBY', KEYS[2], 'shipped', 1) \ return redis.call('LPUSH', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])"; #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders.priority").group("workers"))] async fn ship_first(order: &Order, Ctx(pipeline): Ctx<keys::Pipeline>) -> HandlerOutcome { let touched = vec!["shipments", "orders:totals"]; if pipeline .eval(SHIP_AND_COUNT, touched, vec![order.id.to_string()]) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/redis_pipelining_commands.rs /// The same two writes as one Lua script, so no client sees one without the other. const SHIP_AND_COUNT: &str = "redis.call('HINCRBY', KEYS[2], 'shipped', 1) \ return redis.call('LPUSH', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])"; struct ShipFirst; impl Handle<Order, (), (), PipelineContext> for ShipFirst { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PipelineContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let touched = vec!["shipments", "orders:totals"]; let pipeline = ctx.context(keys::Pipeline); if pipeline .eval(SHIP_AND_COUNT, touched, vec![order.id.to_string()]) .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } }

A window flushes when the read's COUNT has settled, when nothing is outstanding, or when the subscription stops. The flush sends the segments of the acknowledged deliveries, then one pipeline of settles, on a connection of the pool apart from the one the reads block on. A stream's settles leave as one XACK, a reliable list's as one LREM per entry. Under load that is one round trip per fetched batch; on a trickle the window leaves as soon as the last handler of the read returns. What a handler queued follows its delivery's outcome: Outcome The handler's commands The settle ack sent, before the settle the form's own: XACK, LREM drop dropped sent alone retry, retry_after dropped the retry's: the copy or the ZADD, then XACK unsettled dropped none: the entry stays pending Pub/Sub and a simple list settle nothing, so on them every outcome but ack drops the segment. A flush that fails is reported once on the delivery stream, with the subscription, the number of commands and settles it carried, and how many of them failed. On the forms that settle, an entry whose settle failed stays pending and is delivered again. The Window page draws the flush and the Settlement page what each outcome becomes per form. A batch mount's segment is the whole batch. The body's commands and the settles of every entry leave together, and the commands only if every entry is acknowledged. A pipelined reliable list reads its batch with one pipeline of LMOVE, a simple one with RPOP key count. On an empty queue both wait with their blocking pop, BLMOVE or BRPOP, for the next entry.

A batch handler records every order of the batch; one order without items drops the batch, and every push it queued. Macros Manual examples/redis_pipelining_flush.rs /// Records every order of a batch; one order without items drops the batch and its pushes. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"))] async fn accept_all(orders: &[Order], ctx: &mut Context<'_, PipelineContext>) -> HandlerOutcome { let pipeline = ctx.context(keys::Pipeline); for order in orders { if pipeline .lpush("orders:accepted", order.id.to_string()) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } if orders.iter().any(|order| order.items == 0) { tracing::warn!( orders = orders.len(), "a batch with an empty order is dropped" ); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(accept_all.batch(nonzero!(64)).pipeline()) }) } examples/manual/redis_pipelining_flush.rs /// Records every order of a batch; one order without items drops the batch and its pushes. struct AcceptAll; impl Handle<[Order], (), (), PipelineContext> for AcceptAll { async fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PipelineContext>, ) -> Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>> { let pipeline = ctx.context(keys::Pipeline); for order in orders { if pipeline .lpush("orders:accepted", order.id.to_string()) .await .is_err() { return Err(orders.iter().map(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()).collect()); } } if orders.iter().any(|order| order.items == 0) { tracing::warn!( orders = orders.len(), "a batch with an empty order is dropped" ); return Err(orders.iter().map(|_| HandlerOutcome::drop()).collect()); } Ok(()) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { let accept_all = subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"), AcceptAll); b.include(accept_all.batch(nonzero!(64)).pipeline().build()) }, ) }

The InRound transform on the reply position puts a handler's reply into its delivery's round, after the commands it queued. The transform chains after the reply policy: .out_reply(Publish).transform(InRound). The reply then leaves with the delivery's settle, in the window's pipeline, and only when the delivery is acknowledged. It follows what the handler queued and published through a bound slot, so a reader sees the handler's writes in the order the handler made them. Without the transform a reply is an ordinary publish: it leaves as the handler returns, before the window sends what the handler queued. The transform writes the crate's per-message options, so it mounts only where this crate's policies publish.

The reply confirms the order on the same log the bound slot wrote to; with InRound the log reads accepted, then confirmed. Macros Manual examples/redis_pipelining_round.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { // The reply joins the delivery's round after the bound entry, so the log keeps the // order the handler wrote them in. b.include(accept.pipeline()) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(InRound) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish) }, ) } examples/manual/redis_pipelining_round.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { let accept = subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"), Accept); // The reply joins the delivery's round after the bound entry, so the log keeps the // order the handler wrote them in. b.include(accept.pipeline().reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(InRound) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish) }, ) }

RedisGroupPosition names where a consumer group resumes: the oldest retained entry, the tail, or the entry after an id. Constructor Where the group resumes RedisGroupPosition::beginning() the oldest entry the stream still retains RedisGroupPosition::end() the tail: only entries added afterwards RedisGroupPosition::after(id) the entry after that EntryId, which is not delivered again A move is XGROUP SETID, which rewrites the group's cursor. Redis keeps one cursor per group, so a move applies to every consumer of that group, not only to the subscription that asked. A subscription moves its group at startup with start_at, and a handler moves it while the service runs with a seek. A delivery's own position is a RedisGroupPosition too, and moving there delivers that entry again and the entries after it. Streams are the form with a cursor: the core's Seekable capability is implemented for a stream subscription. Where a group starts the first time it is created is its StreamStart.

A producer marks the orders queued behind a marker as void, and the worker moves its group to the tail when it reads the marker. Macros Manual examples/redis_positions_position.rs /// On the void marker the group moves to the tail: the orders queued behind the marker are never /// processed, by this consumer or any other of `workers`. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"))] async fn work(order: &Order, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<keys::SeekHandle>) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.id != 0 { tracing::info!(order.id, "order processed"); return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } match seeker.seek(RedisGroupPosition::end()).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/redis_positions_position.rs /// On the void marker the group moves to the tail: the orders queued behind the marker are never /// processed, by this consumer or any other of `workers`. struct Work; impl Handle<Order, (), (), StreamContext> for Work { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if order.id != 0 { tracing::info!(order.id, "order processed"); return Ok(()); } ctx.context(keys::SeekHandle) .seek(RedisGroupPosition::end()) .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Work).build()) }) }

EntryId is a stream entry's <milliseconds>-<sequence> id; the EntryId key binds the id a delivery was read at. The server assigns the id at XADD. Its first half, milliseconds, is the server clock at that moment. The second, sequence, tells apart the entries added within one millisecond. Ids compare the way the stream orders its entries. EntryId::new(milliseconds, sequence) builds one, and parsing a string checks it, so a value is always a well-formed id. The milliseconds half alone parses too: "1700000000000" is 1700000000000-0. to_string writes the form Redis takes. previous is the id right below, and EntryId::ZERO is below every entry. Ctx<keys::EntryId> binds the id of the delivery, and RedisGroupPosition::after(id) moves a group past it. A batch spans many entries, so a batch context carries no entry id.

Each receipt names the stream entry it billed and when the server added it. Macros Manual examples/redis_positions_entry_id.rs /// The receipt names the entry it bills, so a duplicate bill is traced to one stream entry. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("billing"), reply)] async fn bill(order: &Order, Ctx(entry): Ctx<keys::EntryId>) -> Receipt { tracing::info!(order.id, %entry, "order billed"); Receipt { order: order.id, entry: entry.to_string(), // The first half of the id is the server clock at `XADD`. added_ms: entry.milliseconds(), } } examples/manual/redis_positions_entry_id.rs /// The receipt names the entry it bills, so a duplicate bill is traced to one stream entry. struct Bill; impl Handle<Order, Receipt, (), StreamContext> for Bill { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { let entry = ctx.context(keys::EntryId); tracing::info!(order.id, %entry, "order billed"); ready(Ok(Receipt { order: order.id, entry: entry.to_string(), // The first half of the id is the server clock at `XADD`. added_ms: entry.milliseconds(), })) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = RedisStream::new("orders").group("billing"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Bill).reply().build()) }) }

A handler moves its group's cursor through the SeekHandle key; a delivery's Position key seeks back to that delivery. Ctx<keys::SeekHandle> binds a RedisGroupSeeker for the group the delivery came from. A batch body reads the same key off its StreamBatchContext with ctx.context(keys::SeekHandle). seek(position) takes a RedisGroupPosition and moves the cursor of the whole group, every consumer of it included. The cursor moves as soon as seek returns. A read blocked in XREADGROUP sees the move within one block, and the entries it had selected under the old cursor are discarded, never delivered. Ctx<keys::Position> binds the position of the delivery itself; a seek there delivers that entry again and the entries after it. The group's cursor is exclusive, so that position holds the id one below the entry's, and the crate computes it. A seek leaves three things alone. Entries delivered and not yet acknowledged stay in the pending entries list, where a reclaim subscription can take them. Copies waiting in a delay queue are appended when they fall due, wherever the group reads. A replayed entry is delivered as a new one: Redis starts its delivery count in the pending entries list over at one. So a cap that reads that count, on a claiming or a reclaim subscription, counts from the replay, and the retry-count header the entry carries stays as it was. Seeking is a stream's: a list and a Pub/Sub channel hand each value out once and keep no read position. A seek after the service shut down returns an error. A position that has to hold on every start belongs in start_at.

A batch that holds the void marker moves the group to the tail once it is billed, so the orders queued behind the marker are never billed. Macros Manual examples/redis_positions_seek.rs /// Bills a batch of orders. A batch holding the void marker moves the group to the tail once it /// is billed, so the orders queued behind the marker are never billed. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("billing"))] async fn bill(orders: &[Order], ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamBatchContext>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "orders billed"); if orders.iter().all(|order| order.id != 0) { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } let group = ctx.context(keys::ConsumerGroup); tracing::info!(%group, "void marker, the group moves to the tail"); match ctx .context(keys::SeekHandle) .seek(RedisGroupPosition::end()) .await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/redis_positions_seek.rs /// Bills a batch of orders. A batch holding the void marker moves the group to the tail once it /// is billed, so the orders queued behind the marker are never billed. struct Bill; impl Handle<[Order], (), (), StreamBatchContext> for Bill { async fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamBatchContext>, ) -> Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "orders billed"); if orders.iter().all(|order| order.id != 0) { return Ok(()); } let group = ctx.context(keys::ConsumerGroup); tracing::info!(%group, "void marker, the group moves to the tail"); ctx.context(keys::SeekHandle) .seek(RedisGroupPosition::end()) .await .map_err(|_| orders.iter().map(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()).collect()) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = RedisStream::new("orders").group("billing"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Bill).batch(nonzero!(2)).build()) }) }

start_at moves the group to a position before the first delivery, on every startup; the whole group moves, not one consumer. It is a clause of the attribute, start_at(RedisGroupPosition::beginning()), or .start_at(position) after build() in the manual form. The move happens whatever the group read and acknowledged before. With beginning() the group reads every retained entry again, the acknowledged ones included. Every consumer of the group follows the move, and a consumer blocked in a read sees it within one block. It suits a read model rebuilt from the retained stream on each boot. A StreamStart is different: it applies only when the subscription creates the group. The block step reads the same before and after start_at.

The audit projection is rebuilt from the oldest retained entry on every startup, although its group acknowledged everything it read before. Macros Manual examples/redis_positions_start_at.rs /// Rebuilds the audit projection from the oldest retained entry on every start. The group's /// cursor moves, so every consumer of `projection` replays. #[subscriber( RedisStream::new("audit.trail").group("projection"), start_at(RedisGroupPosition::beginning()) )] async fn project(entry: &AuditEntry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(entry.id, "entry projected"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/redis_positions_start_at.rs /// Projects every audit entry it reads. struct Project; impl Handle<AuditEntry> for Project { fn handle( &self, entry: &AuditEntry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(entry.id, "entry projected"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(url: &str) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone(url), |b| { // The projection is rebuilt from the oldest retained entry on every start. let trail = RedisStream::new("audit.trail").group("projection"); b.include( subscriber(trail, Project) .build() .start_at(RedisGroupPosition::beginning()), ) }) }

RedisPublish, Publish in the stream prelude, appends each message to a stream with XADD. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish) for a slot, .out_retry(Publish) for retry copies. The policy holds no connection and no setting. The runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into a RedisPublisher, so a handler never holds a publisher that is not connected. The message's name is the stream key, and the entry id is *, the one Redis assigns. The payload becomes the entry's _payload field, and each header a field of its own named h:<header>. A publish returns once Redis has answered the XADD. The stream prelude also brings TransactionalPublish, the policy of a mount that publishes in transactions; it pairs into the same publisher, and a cluster refuses it at startup. A list or a channel has its own policy: RedisListPublish and RedisPubSubPublish. A registration that names no policy for its reply publishes through RedisDefaultPublish. Per message, a publish carries a partition key. Outside an app, ConnectedRedisBroker::publisher hands out the same publisher. A reply goes to the stream its type declares with #[outgoing(name = "..")], or to the one the mount site names in reply(".."). Redis carries no reply address and no correlation of its own: a reply is an ordinary publish to a name both sides agree on.

Macros Manual examples/redis_publishing.rs /// The stream a receipt goes to is a property of the type. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order_id: u64, } #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Receipt { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Receipt { order_id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { // Each receipt is an `XADD` to the `receipts` stream. b.include(confirm).out_reply(Publish) }, ) } examples/manual/redis_publishing.rs /// The stream a receipt goes to is a property of the type. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order_id: u64, } struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { let confirm = subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"), Confirm); // Each receipt is an `XADD` to the `receipts` stream. b.include(confirm.reply().build()).out_reply(Publish) }, ) }

A reply with no named policy goes through RedisDefaultPublish, which writes each name the way this service reads it, and XADDs a name it does not read. The runtime wires it for every registration that replies and names no policy: b.include(handler) with no .out_reply(..). Its live form, RedisDefaultPublisher, looks up how the service reads the destination. A name the service reads as a list gets an LPUSH, a channel a PUBLISH, a stream an XADD, each in the envelope that subscription reads. A name the service does not read gets an XADD. The choice is made per name, so one handler's replies may go to a list and another's to a stream. A mount site that names a policy, such as RedisPublish, overrides the default.

The planner replies to jobs without naming a policy; the service reads jobs as a reliable list, so each job is pushed onto it. Macros Manual examples/redis_publishing_default.rs /// Plans a job per order; the reply names no policy. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("planners"), reply)] async fn plan(order: &Order) -> Job { Job { order_id: order.id } } /// Pops the jobs off the `jobs` list. #[subscriber(RedisList::new("jobs").reliable())] async fn work(job: &Job) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.order_id, "job done"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("jobs", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { // `jobs` is a list this service reads, so the default publisher pushes onto it. b.include(plan).include(work) }, ) } examples/manual/redis_publishing_default.rs /// Plans a job per order; the reply names no policy. struct Plan; impl Handle<Order, Job> for Plan { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Job, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Job { order_id: order.id })) } } /// Pops the jobs off the `jobs` list. struct Work; impl Handle<Job> for Work { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.order_id, "job done"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("jobs", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { let plan = subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("planners"), Plan); // `jobs` is a list this service reads, so the default publisher pushes onto it. b.include(plan.reply().build()) .include(subscriber(RedisList::new("jobs").reliable(), Work).build()) }, ) }

RedisListPublish, Publish in the list prelude, pushes with LPUSH and can re-arm a key expiry at every publish. The message's name is the list key. A list consumer pops from the other end, so the list is a first-in, first-out queue. Headers travel beside the payload in the broker's envelope; envelope names another, which the consumer reads too. ttl sets a time to live on the list key and arms it again with PEXPIRE at every publish. A queue in use never expires; a queue nobody pushes to for the whole interval does, with whatever it still holds. The expiry is the key's: Redis lists expire as a whole, never per element. The push and the PEXPIRE leave in one round trip but are two commands, not one transaction. The policy pairs into a RedisListPublisher at startup.

Each order asks for a shipping label on the label-jobs list, whose key expires after an hour without a push. Macros Manual examples/redis_publishing_list.rs #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("labels"), reply)] async fn request_label(order: &Order) -> LabelJob { LabelJob { order_id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // A queue nobody drains for an hour expires instead of growing. let jobs = list::Publish::new().ttl(Duration::from_secs(3600)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("labels", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(request_label).out_reply(jobs) }) } examples/manual/redis_publishing_list.rs struct RequestLabel; impl Handle<Order, LabelJob> for RequestLabel { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<LabelJob, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(LabelJob { order_id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { // A queue nobody drains for an hour expires instead of growing. let jobs = list::Publish::new().ttl(Duration::from_secs(3600)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("labels", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { let request = subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("labels"), RequestLabel); b.include(request.reply().build()).out_reply(jobs) }, ) }

partition_key keys one message, so workers(n, by_key) on the consuming side keeps the order of messages sharing that key. workers(n, by_key) runs a subscription on n lanes, and deliveries with one partition key always share a lane. The key travels in the PARTITION_KEY_HEADER header, which is where the consuming side reads it. Writing that header at the call site works the same, and carries across brokers. The step goes anywhere after .message(..) on the publish builder, so it composes with a header contract the message type declares. It writes through RedisPublishOptions, the per-message options of every publisher in this crate. The slot is bounded as Out<impl Publisher<Options = RedisPublishOptions>, Slot>, which keeps the step off another broker's publisher. Naming that type is the one case where a handler body imports this crate's prelude instead of the framework's alone. A publish without the step carries no options and leaves the headers as they are.

The intake forwards each order keyed by its customer; the ledger books on four lanes, and one customer's orders keep their order. Macros Manual examples/redis_publishing_partition_key.rs /// Forwards each order keyed by its customer. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders.in").group("intake"))] async fn forward( order: &Order, Out(ledger): Out<impl Publisher<Options = RedisPublishOptions>, Ledger>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let keyed = KeyedOrder { id: order.id, customer: order.customer.clone(), }; let published = ledger .message(&keyed) .partition_key(order.customer.as_str()) .publish() .await; if published.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Four lanes; the orders of one customer share a lane and keep their order. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders.keyed").group("ledger"), workers(4, by_key))] async fn book(order: &KeyedOrder) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, order.customer, "order booked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(forward) .out(Ledger, Publish) .build() .include(book) }, ) } examples/manual/redis_publishing_partition_key.rs /// Forwards each order keyed by its customer. struct Forward; impl<L> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(L,)>> for Forward where L: OutEntry<Ledger, Wire: Publisher<Options = RedisPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(L,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let keyed = KeyedOrder { id: order.id, customer: order.customer.clone(), }; outs.get(Ledger) .message(&keyed) .partition_key(order.customer.as_str()) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } /// Books an order; the lanes keep one customer's orders in order. struct Book; impl Handle<KeyedOrder> for Book { fn handle( &self, order: &KeyedOrder, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, order.customer, "order booked"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { let forward = subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders.in").group("intake"), Forward); // Four lanes; the orders of one customer share a lane and keep their order. let book = subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders.keyed").group("ledger"), Book); b.include(forward.build()) .out(Ledger, Publish) .build() .include(book.workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)).build()) }, ) }

RedisPubSubPublish, Publish in the Pub/Sub prelude, sends with PUBLISH or SPUBLISH in the envelope it names. The message's name is the channel. mode picks the command: PubSubMode::Classic, the default, sends PUBLISH, and PubSubMode::Sharded sends SPUBLISH to the channel's slot. The mode matches the subscribers': a sharded message reaches only SSUBSCRIBE subscriptions. Headers travel beside the payload in the broker's envelope. envelope names another, such as a JSON document readable as text; the subscribers read the same envelope. A payload that is not text is published byte for byte either way. The policy pairs into a RedisPubSubPublisher at startup. A message reaches the subscriptions connected when it is sent; Redis keeps no copy for a subscriber that connects later. A publish to a channel nobody hears succeeds.

Each event is answered with an audit entry, sent with PUBLISH to the audit channel its type declares.
